summary: Korean yakisoba: fresh yakisoba noodles stir-fried with browned tofu, shishito peppers, asparagus and garlic chives in a hatcho miso, gochujang and mirin sauce, topped with seared king oyster mushrooms, quick radish kimchi, shiso and a 5:10 egg; serves 4, and a 30-minute meal if simplified.
glance: 1/4 cup hatcho miso (or red miso), 1/4 cup gochujang, 1/2 cup mirin, toasted sesame oil, lemon zest
5 minutes 10 seconds in a simmer, then ice bath
Vegetarian and kosher (gochujang often contains wheat)
faq: What is gochujang?

A mainstay of Korean cuisine: a hot paste made from spicy peppers, rice and fermented soybeans, often with some wheat products (not gluten-free). It keeps a long time in the fridge, and the author guarantees you'll be addicted after one try.
What is hatcho miso?
Almost black, chunky and fudgy, with a somewhat smoky taste. If you can't find it, use a red miso.
How do I make the quick radish kimchi?

Toss thinly sliced red radishes with sliced garlic, salt, sugar and Korean red pepper powder (or cayenne) and rest at room temperature about an hour; it can be made a day ahead. In Korea kimchi is made from anything from cabbage to pears, so it's a template for many vegetables, adding acidity and crunch.
How do I make the 5:10 egg?

David Chang's approach: lower refrigerator-temperature eggs into a simmering pot for exactly 5 minutes 10 seconds, then transfer to an ice bath and peel. Cut halfway through at serving so the yolk slowly runs out. You may want extra eggs to be safe.
Can I simplify it?

Yes: just noodles tossed with the sauce, whatever vegetables you want and jarred kimchi is easily a 30-minute meal. Garlic chives (nira) can be replaced with 6-8 scallions, and French horn mushrooms are king oyster mushrooms.

summary: Pomegranate-glazed freekeh kofte, vegetarian "meatballs": freekeh simmered about 50 minutes, cooled and mixed with roasted eggplant, egg, ras el hanout and breadcrumbs, shaped into 1 1/2-inch balls, shallow-fried about 2 minutes per side and brushed with pomegranate molasses; makes about 12.
glance: 1 cup, toasted then simmered about 50 minutes in 2 1/3 cups water
1/4 inch of oil, about 2 minutes per side, internal temperature at least 155°F
1/3 cup pomegranate molasses, brushed on after frying
faq: What is freekeh?

Wheat harvested while still green, sun-dried and lightly roasted by burning the chaff and stalks around it, used in the Middle East and North Africa for centuries in spiced pilafs, stuffings, soups and stews. Both the greenness and the roasting give an aroma unlike anything else.
What is kofte?
A little meatball or patty; here the vegetarian version of "meatballs" uses the coarse texture of freekeh to stay loosely bound rather than becoming overly dense.
How do I keep the kofte from being dense?
Mix with your hands without smushing everything together too much, and shape gently into 1 1/2-inch balls.
How do I know they're cooked?
With an instant-read thermometer, check that they reach an internal temperature of at least 155°F. Fry about 2 minutes per side, adjusting the heat so they brown but don't burn.
Can I change the flavors?
Fennel seeds and garlic with tomato sauce would give an Italian approach; here ras el hanout and pomegranate molasses keep a Middle Eastern profile. Serve immediately since they soften if they sit.

summary: Sopes with plantain, zucchini and two sauces: masa discs griddled 10 seconds a side, pinched into a rim, finished 1 minute and shallow-fried 45-60 seconds, topped with a caramelized plantain, zucchini and onion filling, a smoky guajillo salsa and a charred scallion and lime sour cream; makes 16, 90 minutes.
glance: salsa and sour cream a day or two ahead; filling a day ahead; shells a few hours ahead
2 1/2 cups masa harina, 1 3/4 cups hot water, shortening, flour, baking powder; rest 30 minutes
Kosher; vegan with a vegan sour cream
faq: What are antojitos and sopes?

Antojitos are a class of Mexican street food dishes (also smaller appetizers at restaurants), most of which include a corn masa component. Sopes are a classic antojito made by griddling a thick tortilla, reshaping it with a rim, then shallow frying to crisp it.
How do I shape sopes?

Press a 1 1/4-inch ball into a 3 1/2-inch round about 1/4 inch thick, griddle 10 seconds per side, cool a few seconds, and pinch dough from the middle out into walls about 1/4 inch thick and 1/2 inch high. Return to the griddle flat side only for one minute, then fry wall side down 45-60 seconds.
Green or ripe plantains?
The author first used green, starchy plantains (like potato), but recommends ripe plantains, whose sweetness makes the dish even better.
How do I make the sauces?

Guajillo salsa: toast dried guajillos and unpeeled garlic about 5 minutes, seed and blend with Muir Glen fire-roasted tomatoes, salt and sugar. Sour cream: char scallions in a skillet and blend with sour cream, cilantro, lime juice and salt.
Can I simplify the project?
Yes: make both sauces and the filling ahead so you only concentrate on the sope shells on the day. All it needs is guacamole, black or pinto beans and maybe a salad.

summary: Vegetarian ceviche, a composed salad with a citrus-only dressing: oyster mushrooms, hearts of palm rings, radish, cucumber, jalapeno and red onion marinated a couple of minutes in lime and Meyer lemon juice, finished with sea salt, mint or cilantro and tortilla chips for crunch; vegan, serves 4.
glance: juice of 1 lime and 1 Meyer lemon with a bit of salt, a couple of minutes
tortilla chips (or spiced popcorn, roasted corn kernels or fried plantains)
faq: What is traditional ceviche?
Raw or lightly cooked fish and shellfish marinated in citrus juices, served throughout Latin America, with each country adding its own twists on the ingredients, sauce or crispy accompaniments.
How do you make a vegetarian version?

Think in terms of a composed salad with tropical and spicy elements and a dressing of citrus with no oil. The author used oyster mushrooms and (sustainably harvested) hearts of palm as somewhat humorous seafood references: the mushrooms by name and the palm by shape.
What crunchy element goes with it?

Ceviche usually includes something salty and crispy for contrast: roasted corn kernels (like Corn Nuts), popcorn or fried plantains. The author used tortilla chips but would have preferred spiced-up popcorn.
How long do I marinate it?

Toss the vegetables with the salted citrus juice and let marinate for just a couple of minutes, then divide into serving vessels making sure each gets an oyster mushroom, and drizzle on a bit of the juice.
When do I serve it?
With cocktails, or as the first course of a dinner party.

summary: Shaved artichoke salad with blood oranges: raw artichoke hearts shaved on a mandoline and tossed immediately in a blood orange juice and mayonnaise dressing (reminiscent of celery root remoulade), mounded on chilled plates with orange supremes, chives and flaky salt; serves 4 in 15 minutes.
glance: 1 tablespoon blood orange juice, 1/4 cup mayonnaise, salt, optional ras el hanout; make first
2 large globe artichokes with 3-inch stems, trimmed to the heart
faq: Can you eat artichokes raw?

Yes: artichokes are almost always served cooked, but raw they taste like a slightly astringent root vegetable. A lemony vinaigrette and shards of Parmigiano-Reggiano work, or this mayonnaise-based dressing for a salad reminiscent of celery root remoulade.
How do I keep the artichoke from browning?
Prepare the dressing first so you can toss the shaved artichoke in it immediately, and work quickly.
How do I prepare the artichokes?

Trim a bit off the stems and peel them, pull off all the leaves (steam them separately if you like), remove the hairy choke with a spoon, and peel and pare around the artichoke bottom, leaving the peeled stem attached to a trimmed heart. Slice thinly on a mandoline, which gives thinner, more even slices than a knife.
What are citrus supremes?

A citrus segment free of any membrane or white pith: beautiful and more intense in taste. Slice off the top and bottom, trim away the skin and pith, then cut in on both sides of each segment as close to the membrane as possible over a bowl. Use intact peeled segments if you're uncomfortable with the knife technique.
Can I use other oranges?
Blood oranges are in season in winter; any other orange works, though you'll miss the visual interest of the bright red segments.

summary: Lychee tempura, the second of three lychee amuse bouche: halved, pitted lychees dredged in flour and a small-batch tempura batter (from Morimoto) and fried at 350°F until golden, served with a togarashi mayo, black sea salt and a lemon wedge; serves 4 as an amuse bouche.
glance: 1 egg yolk, 1/4 cup oil, 3/4 cup cold club soda, 1 cup flour; don't overbeat
1 inch of oil at 350°F, golden brown, drained immediately
black sea salt, togarashi mayo, lemon wedge
faq: Where does the batter come from?

The small-batch tempura batter is from Morimoto: The New Art of Japanese Cooking: an egg yolk whisked successively with vegetable oil, cold club soda and flour. It shouldn't be too thick, so thin with a bit more soda if necessary, and don't overbeat.
What temperature should the oil be?
350°F in a very small pot with 1 inch of oil. Don't overheat or it will develop unpleasant flavors and be a fire risk.
How do I fry lychees?

Using chopsticks, dredge each peeled, halved and pitted lychee in flour, then in the tempura batter, shake off the excess and lower into the oil; fry until golden brown, turning if needed, and drain on paper towels. Serve immediately.
What is togarashi mayo?
1 tablespoon of mayonnaise mixed with about 1/2 teaspoon of shichimi (nanami) togarashi pepper, served in half-teaspoon dabs with black sea salt and a small lemon wedge.
What is the story behind it?
The author recalls a tempura-only counter restaurant in Tokyo with ten seats, where the chef made vegetarian courses (especially maitake) with just sea salt to touch each bite.

summary: Couscous with parsley-yogurt sauce, spicy acorn squash, roasted cauliflower and chickpeas: four components made separately (a food-processor parsley and Greek yogurt sauce, harissa-rubbed squash and cauliflower roasted at 400°F, cumin chickpeas with onion, and fluffy couscous); serves 4.
glance: 1 acorn squash with 1 tablespoon dry harissa, roasted at 400°F about 15 minutes
3 cups plain Greek yogurt, 1 big bunch parsley, garlic, lemon, blended
Vegetarian, not gluten-free; vegan with soy yogurt
faq: Why make a parsley yogurt sauce?

It can be made in minutes in a food processor and amps up the flavor of any meal, and is especially welcome with spicy foods because the yogurt cuts the heat. The same sauce can work as a salad dressing or even a cold soup.
Can I use other herbs?
Yes: mint, dill, oregano, marjoram or scallions, alone or in combination. Add grated, seeded cucumber and you're headed into Indian raita territory.
Does the yogurt need draining?
No: Greek God's yogurt is thick and flavorful, so no draining is required. Its plain or non-fat versions are excellent for cooking.
Why separate sub-recipes?

The author separated the components to make it easier to do parts ahead or mix and match. Oven-roasting gives the vegetables a light caramelization, and the harissa rub gives the squash another dimension.
How do I make the couscous fluffy?
1.5 cups couscous with 2 1/4 cups water and salt, following the author's fluffy couscous method (pouring boiling water over couscous spread thin in a casserole and covering).

summary: Banana raita: diced ripe banana tossed with lemon juice and folded into smooth beaten yogurt with salt, sugar, popped black mustard seeds, jalapeno and green onion; gluten-free, 5 minutes, makes 1 1/2 cups of a cooling Indian condiment that tastes like a banana smoothie with a surprise.
glance: 1 tablespoon, cooked in hot oil about 1 minute until they pop and change color
faq: What is raita?

A family of yogurt-based condiments that go with just about any Indian dish, from street food to a sumptuous banquet, making a cooling complement to a spicy dish. Only cucumber raita has become popular in America.
Why banana?
The flavors are at once familiar and surprising: first you get banana smoothie, then your taste buds are surprised by mustard seed, jalapeno and spring onion.
How do I keep the banana from browning?
Toss the finely diced ripe banana with the lemon juice.
How do I make it?

Beat 1 cup of yogurt with salt and sugar until smooth, then mix in the bananas, the mustard seeds popped in hot oil and the optional jalapeno. Taste, adjust, and garnish with thinly sliced green onion.
What does it go with?
The author suggests aloo tikki; it's a cooling complement to any spicy dish.

summary: Baked eggs with chanterelles and chard: a crustless brunch dish of 10 eggs, milk and creme fraiche mixed with sauteed chanterelles, onion and wilted chard, topped with Parmesan and baked at 350°F for about 50 minutes in a 10-inch deep dish; serves 4-6 and is good at room temperature.
glance: 350°F for about 50 minutes, until well browned and a toothpick comes out dry
10 eggs with 2 cups milk and 1 cup creme fraiche
2 pounds chanterelles, sauteed about 10 minutes until all water cooks off
faq: Why bake eggs for brunch?
Baked egg dishes are ideal for brunch with friends, especially with kids who won't wait patiently while you cook 30 pancakes.
Why add creme fraiche?
The author learned it from the amazing quiche in the Tartine cookbook. His version is crustless and closer to scrambled eggs than a custard, with a very mild tang and richness.
Can I add cheese or use other mushrooms?

Mix in a cup of any meltable cheese such as Gruyere or Appenzeller for more flavor. If you can't find chanterelles, use another wild mushroom or even cultivated mushrooms, cooking off all of the liquid.
How do I prepare the mushrooms and chard?

Saute the onion 2 minutes, then the chanterelles, garlic and salt about 10 minutes until golden, somewhat tender and dry. In the same skillet wilt the chard ribbons (covering part of the time to speed it) and mix with the mushrooms.
How should I serve it?
After cooling at least 15 minutes, or at room temperature.

summary: Brussels sprouts with seeds and coconut, an Indian-style side: sprouts shredded, microwaved or steamed 4 minutes, then stir-fried 2 minutes with ghee, optional urad dal, mustard, black caraway and cumin seeds, toasted coconut, jaggery, garam masala and lime; serves 4 as a side dish.
glance: 3 cups, trimmed and sliced thin; pre-cooked 4 minutes until nearly tender
about 2 minutes after the seeds pop
black mustard, black caraway, cumin; optional urad dal
Vegetarian and gluten-free; vegan with oil instead of butter
faq: Why mustard seeds with Brussels sprouts?
Mustard and Brussels sprouts are both in the brassica family, so the seeds really complement the flavor.
How do I avoid unpleasant sulfury flavors?
The key, as with anything in the cabbage world, is not to overcook them: microwave or steam the sliced sprouts just 4 minutes until nearly tender, then stir-fry only 2 minutes.
What is urad dal for?
An optional type of Indian split pea fried until it turns reddish brown (a couple of minutes), which adds an additional crunchy element.
Can I add other flavorings?
Fresh green chilis, ginger, garlic or onions would all be welcome.
What did the author serve it with?
Basmati rice, aloo gobi (potato and cauliflower curry), cucumber raita and papadums.
